newsitem.title: USA: U.S. savings rate edges up, suggesting trend.
newsitem.headline: U.S. savings rate edges up, suggesting trend.

text.p: Americans are stashing away more of what they earn, new data show, suggesting they may be getting more serious about saving for their retirement years.

Savings rose to 5.7 cents out of each dollar earned in September from 5.2 cents in August, the Commerce Department reported Thursday. That's the highest level since December 1993, when the savings rate stood at 6.3 percent.
While economists warn that the figures tend to behave erratically and can be revised, some forecasters said the recent data could prove to be the start of a long-term trend.

"I think what we may be on is the leading edge of a decision to save a little bit more," said Joel L. Naroff, chief bank economist at First Union Corp. in Philadelphia. "You can't expect a sudden groundswell to occur."
The national savings rate is likely getting a boost as retirement nears for the first members of the baby boom generation -- those born between the years of 1946 and 1964.

"I absolutely see this as a trend," said David Wray, president of the Profit Sharing/401(k) Council of America, which represents companies offering those benefits. "We will see the savings rate continue to improve."
Younger savers, fearing that the social security system may go bust before they retire, are also socking away cash and contributing to the overall push to save more.
"Younger people are much more aware today that they need to save for retirement than they were at any time in history," Wray said.
The stock market's meteoric rise has also encouraged consumers to save money by investing in mutual funds.
Despite the improvement, economists maintain that the savings rate remains too low, especially for those baby boomers that started saving late.

"It's not adequate if you believe the purchasing power of what they receive from social security is going to be small," said Paul Taylor, senior economist at America's Community Bankers, a trade group for thrifts and savings banks. "There will be so many of them the system will be under pressure."
Other theories abound about why the data showed strength.

Ken Goldstein, an economist at The Conference Board, speculated that older baby boomers may be "empty nesters" now. "They're still spending the way they used to spend but don't have to spend for their kids so at least for the moment they're parking money," Goldstein said.

That may bode well for retailers during the holidays, he said. "They have more money to spend and they're willing to spend it," Goldstein said. "This may be the best holiday season for retailers in the last five years."

Huge consumer debt levels may also be a driving force behind the September savings phenomenon as consumers are "trying not to add to their credit cards and lenders are not extending new credit quite as freely," said Sandra Shaber, consumer analyst at the WEFA Group.

Shaber contended that the upward blip in the savings rate is not yet sustainable. "We haven't seen any real behavioral changes in what people are doing to announce that we're going to have a real upward push," she said.
But some say the message may be starting to sink in.
"It's a step in the right direction -- people are starting to get religion," said J Carter Beese Jr., vice chairman of Alex. Brown & Sons International.
"People need to start saving from the time they enter the work force," said Beese, who repeatedly drew attention to the issue when he served on the Securities and Exchange Commission.
